analysis.one_liner: Requires warehouse employers to disclose work quotas, guarantee paid rest breaks, and set safety standards.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 50 cosponsors including 3 Republicans, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Warehouse Worker Protection Act would have required warehouse and fulfillment-center employers to give workers written notice of any work quotas, the surveillance technology used to track them, and the data collected on them. It would ban quotas that cut into legally required breaks or bathroom time, guarantee a paid 15-minute rest break for every 4 hours of work, and require written notice before firing a worker. It would also direct OSHA to write ergonomics standards to prevent the muscle and joint injuries common in warehouse work, and it would bar companies from forcing workers into arbitration over quota violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Warehouse and fulfillment-center workers — a workforce of well over a million people concentrated in large logistics operations — who face injury-prone pace targets, algorithmic tracking, and discipline based on speed data they often cannot see or contest.

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to disclose each quota, the discipline tied to missing it, how targets are calculated, and what surveillance technology and data collection are used to monitor the worker [S2].

Quotas could not prevent legally required breaks, bathroom use with reasonable travel time, or reasonable accommodations, and discipline could not rest solely on ranking a worker against peers or on continuous second-by-second tracking [S2].

Workers would get a paid 15-minute rest break for every 4 hours of work, plus the right to see, supplement, and dispute the speed data kept on them, and to request copies during and after employment [S2].

Employers could not fire a worker without written notice (except for egregious misconduct), and retaliation against workers exercising these rights would carry a rebuttable presumption against the employer if it happened within 90 days [S2].

OSHA would be required to write standards on ergonomics and on prompt medical referral after injuries, and serious, willful, or repeated safety violations would have to be corrected even while an employer contests the citation [S2].
Predispute arbitration agreements could not be enforced against claims under the quota protections, and workers would gain a simplified path to bring group claims [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large warehouse, fulfillment, and courier operators — the bill covers warehousing, wholesale distribution, electronic shopping and mail-order retail, and express delivery facilities — which would bear the cost of disclosure, recordkeeping, paid breaks, and slower firing procedures.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on covered employers: a new federal office, mandatory written disclosures, record retention for at least 3 years, and paid rest breaks all carry real administrative and payroll costs that could weigh most on smaller warehouse operations [S2].

The quota definition is broad — covering any quantified target measured within a day — so employers would face uncertainty about which routine performance practices count as regulated quotas and might restructure incentives rather than improve conditions [S2].

Requiring written notice before any termination (with a misconduct exception) and a rebuttable presumption of retaliation after protected activity would make firing decisions slower and more contestable, which employers would argue raises litigation risk [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the bill addresses well-documented conditions — injury-prone pace targets, opaque algorithmic monitoring, and race-to-the-bottom discipline — with notice rights, enforceable breaks, and safety standards. The costs are compliance burdens on employers, and the biggest question mark is whether the very broad quota definition creates more paperwork than protection. On balance the benefits for workers are large and the costs are real but targeted at an industry with above-average injury rates.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross (D-NJ) introduced the bill on June 5, 2024, with 24 original cosponsors from both parties [S1][S2].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction, and the action history records no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S4].
Cosponsorship grew to 50 members — 47 of 216 House Democrats and 3 of 224 House Republicans — but the committee never acted [S3].
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, so all legislation not passed, including this bill, expired [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large warehouse and e-commerce logistics operators, which keep their quota systems, speed-tracking technology, and arbitration requirements untouched by federal law.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 47 of 216 House Democrats versus 3 of 224 House Republicans — and the Republican-run committee and House leadership took no action on it.

industries.industry: Warehousing and e-commerce fulfillment (Amazon-type operations, covered by NAICS 493, 423, 424, and 454110)
industries.note: The bill would have required these operators to disclose quotas and surveillance, restrict how speed data can be used in discipline, guarantee paid breaks, and slow terminations — direct limits on a business model built on quantified pace targets. Its gain in keeping the status quo came at the cost of workers' transparency and break rights.
Explicitly covered facilities would have faced the same quota-disclosure, break, and safety-standard requirements, raising labor costs in a sector with high injury rates.
The bill defines covered employers to include staffing agencies and leasing entities, so they would share the compliance burden alongside the warehouses they staff.
